question: How should oxygen be viewed when given to a patient in the hospital?

options.A: As a basic comfort measure that needs no order
options.B: As a routine supplement for every admitted patient
options.C: As a medical drug requiring a proper prescription
options.D: As a permanent fluid replacement therapy

explanation: Oxygen acts as a pharmacological agent and must be prescribed by a clinician with specific flow rates and delivery methods to avoid misuse. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why is giving extra oxygen so important during severe bleeding in pregnancy?

options.A: To maintain adequate oxygen delivery to vital organs and the fetus
options.B: To immediately stop the underlying uterine bleeding
options.C: To prevent the sudden rise of maternal blood pressure
options.D: To replace the lost volume of circulating blood plasma

explanation: Blood loss reduces the body's oxygen-carrying capacity. Supplemental oxygen helps maximize the remaining hemoglobin's saturation to protect both mother and baby. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which oxygen mask uses color-coded valves to supply a precise, fixed amount of oxygen?
explanation: The Venturi system uses specific jet adapters or valves to mix exact amounts of room air with oxygen, guaranteeing a precise concentration. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the most important safety rule when setting up an oxygen cylinder in a ward?

options.A: Placing a portable heater right beside the tank to keep the oxygen warm
options.B: Laying the heavy metal cylinder flat on the floor under the bed
options.C: Lubricating the flowmeter valve with petroleum jelly to prevent leaks
options.D: Securing the cylinder upright and keeping it away from oil and naked flames

explanation: Upright storage prevents falling injuries, and avoiding oils or open flames is vital because oxygen intensely feeds fire. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which device gives a quick, non-invasive check of a patient's blood oxygen level?
explanation: A pulse oximeter clips onto a finger or earlobe to read light absorption, estimating the percentage of oxygen-saturated hemoglobin. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why is water added to oxygen setups that run at higher flow rates?

options.A: To cool the oxygen down to freezing temperatures
options.B: To prevent the drying and irritation of the patient's nasal and airway mucosa
options.C: To increase the total percentage of oxygen coming out of the wall outlet
options.D: To add extra moisture to the room air for other patients

explanation: Dry medical gases strip moisture from the respiratory tract, causing discomfort and crusting unless humidified. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the main job of bronchodilator medications?

options.A: Relaxing the smooth muscles around the airways to ease breathing
options.B: Lowering the patient's systemic blood pressure during stress
options.C: Increasing the overall red blood cell count in the bloodstream
options.D: Drying up excessive mucus secretions in the upper nasal passages

explanation: Bronchodilators target the smooth muscle layers in bronchial tubes, causing them to dilate and open constricted airways. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h4)

question: How does a Dry Powder Inhaler (DPI) work differently from a standard Metered-Dose Inhaler (MDI)?

options.A: A DPI uses a propellant gas to push the medicine out automatically
options.B: A DPI requires a spacer device attached at all times to work properly
options.C: A DPI is only used for oxygen delivery rather than medication
options.D: A DPI is activated entirely by the force of the patient's own deep inhalation

explanation: While MDIs rely on propellant sprays and coordination, DPIs depend on the patient generating a strong, fast breath to aerosolize the powder. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is the main benefit of using a spacer with a Metered-Dose Inhaler?

options.A: It turns liquid medications into intravenous solutions automatically
options.B: It overcomes poor hand-breath coordination by holding the spray in a chamber
options.C: It speeds up the heart rate so the drug absorbs faster
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any prescription from a doctor

explanation: Spacers capture the medication cloud so patients do not have to press the canister and breathe in at the exact same millisecond. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h5)

question: What should you tell a patient to do if a whistling sound is heard while breathing in through a spacer?

options.A: Slow down and breathe in less forcefully
options.B: Stop the treatment immediately and call for emergency help
options.C: Inhale much faster and harder to clear the blockage
options.D: Shake the inhaler harder while still holding it in the mouth

explanation: A whistle indicates that the breathing rate is too fast, meaning the medicine might hit the back of the throat instead of entering the lungs. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h5)

question: What must a patient do immediately after using a corticosteroid inhaler?

options.A: Apply antiseptic ointment directly onto the tongue surface
options.B: Rinse the mouth thoroughly with water and spit it out
options.C: Brush the teeth vigorously with hard abrasive toothpaste
options.D: Swallow a large glass of milk to coat the stomach lining

explanation: Rinsing removes residual steroid particles left in the mouth, preventing fungal infections like thrush and throat irritation. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good teaching method when showing a patient how to use a new inhaler?

options.A: Asking the patient to demonstrate the technique back to the nurse
options.B: Providing a written action plan for worsening breathing symptoms
options.C: Explaining the purpose of the medication in simple local terms
options.D: Relying entirely on a complex medical pamphlet without discussion

explanation: Handing out dense pamphlets without verbal explanation or return demonstration often leads to improper use and poor compliance. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h6)

question: What problem can happen if very high oxygen concentrations are given for too long?

options.A: Permanent discoloration of the skin and nail beds
options.B: Instantaneous lowering of body temperature and shivering
options.C: Alveolar membrane damage and oxygen toxicity
options.D: Severe iron-deficiency anemia due to red blood cell destruction

explanation: Prolonged exposure to high levels of oxygen generates free radicals that injure lung tissues and alveolar walls. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which side effect do patients often feel after taking a fast-acting bronchodilator inhaler?

options.C: Sudden severe drop in body weight
options.D: Total loss of the sense of taste

explanation: Beta-agonist bronchodilators can cross into the bloodstream and stimulate receptors in the heart, causing temporary fast heart rates. [learn more](BMP125_U1_T10#BMP125_U1_T10_h7)
